text_blocks.snippet: Both Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) are effective, guideline-recommended first-line medications for treating high blood pressure, though ARBs are generally preferred today due to a better side-effect profile .
snippet_highlighted_words: ARBs are generally preferred today due to a better side-effect profile

list.snippet: Blood Pressure Control: Both drug classes lower blood pressure by acting on the body's renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).

Cardiovascular Protection: Large clinical studies and meta-analyses show no significant difference between the two classes in preventing major events like heart attacks, strokes, or heart failure hospitalizations.
Affordability: Generic options for both ACE inhibitors and ARBs are widely available at a low cost.

Mechanism: ACE inhibitors block the enzyme that produces angiotensin II. ARBs block the angiotensin II receptors directly. ACE inhibitors also lead to a buildup of bradykinin, which causes unique side effects.

Side Effects (Cough and Angioedema): ACE inhibitors frequently cause a nagging, dry cough (in up to 10% or more of patients) and carry a higher risk of angioedema (dangerous tissue swelling, particularly of the face or throat). ARBs do not trigger the bradykinin buildup, resulting in a much lower incidence of cough and angioedema.
Adherence: Because ARBs are much better tolerated, patients are less likely to stop taking them compared to ACE inhibitors.

First-Line Preference: Insights shared via the American Academy of Family Physicians (AFP) and large-scale data reviews discussed on note that while international guidelines traditionally gave both classes equal weight, modern clinical practice leans toward starting with an ARB to avoid side effects.

Switching: If you are already taking an ACE inhibitor and your blood pressure is well-controlled without a cough or other issues, doctors generally do not need to switch you to an ARB. However, if you develop an ACE-inhibitor-induced dry cough, switching to an ARB is a standard and effective solution.
Note: You should never take an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together, as combination therapy increases the risk of high potassium and kidney dysfunction without added cardiovascular benefit.
